{{Short description|Theorem in group theory}}
In [[mathematics|mathematical]] [[group theory]], the '''Hall&ndash;Higman theorem''', due to {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Philip Hall|first=Philip|last=Hall|first2=Graham|last2=Higman|author2-link=Graham Higman||year=1956|loc=Theorem B}}, describes the possibilities for the [[minimal polynomial (linear algebra)|minimal polynomial]] of an element of [[prime power]] order for a [[Group representation|representation]] of a [[p-solvable group|''p''-solvable group]].

==Statement==

Suppose that ''G'' is a ''p''-solvable group with no normal ''p''-subgroups, [[acting faithfully]] on a [[vector space]] over a [[field characteristic|field of characteristic]] ''p''. 
If ''x'' is an element of order ''p''<sup>''n''</sup> of ''G'' then the minimal polynomial is of the form (''X''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1)<sup>''r''</sup> for some ''r''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''p''<sup>''n''</sup>. The Hall&ndash;Higman theorem states that one of the following 3 possibilities holds:
*''r''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''p''<sup>''n''</sup>
*''p'' is a [[Fermat prime]] and the [[Sylow 2-subgroup]]s of ''G'' are [[Non-abelian group|non-abelian]] and ''r''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;''p''<sup>''n''</sup> &minus;''p''<sup>''n''&minus;1</sup>
*''p''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2 and the Sylow ''q''-subgroups of ''G'' are non-abelian for some [[Mersenne prime]] ''q''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2<sup>''m''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 less than 2<sup>''n''</sup> and ''r''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;2<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;2<sup>''n''&minus;''m''</sup>.

==Examples==
The group [[Special linear group|SL<sub>2</sub>]]('''F'''<sub>3</sub>) is 3-solvable (in fact [[Solvable group|solvable]]) and has an obvious 2-dimensional representation over a field of characteristic ''p''=3, in which the elements of order 3 have minimal polynomial (''X''&minus;1)<sup>2</sup> with ''r''=3&minus;1.
